cards.front: Recall a key point about Mark Making and Line
cards.back: Different types of line serve different purposes: contour lines define edges, gestural lines capture movement, analytical lines record accurate proportions.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Mark Making and Line
cards.back: Mark-making is the foundation of drawing — experiment with pressure, speed, direction and media to create varied marks.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Mark Making and Line
cards.back: Hatching and cross-hatching build tone through overlapping lines; stippling uses dots; both can describe form and texture.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Mark Making and Line
cards.back: Expressive line can convey emotion and energy; analytical line prioritises accuracy and measurement.

cards.front: What should you know about fine art exam tips?
cards.back: Show a RANGE of mark types — don't just use one approach. Annotate your experiments explaining WHY you chose each mark. Link your mark-making to specific artists. Show how marks evolved from initial experiments to final piece.

Students often make mistakes with this topic. Wrong: Only tight, photorealistic drawing counts as good drawing. Correct: Drawing for different purposes — expressive, gestural, analytical — all have value. AQA says drawing should address purpose and need, not just technical mastery unless that is your intention.
Analyse how two different artists use line and mark-making. Compare their approaches and explain how this research has influenced your own mark-making experiments.

cards.front: Assessment Objective Focus: Mark Making and Line
cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Mark Making and Line using appropriate art vocabulary. Identify techniques, materials and processes accurately.

cards.front: Understanding Mark Making and Line in Context
cards.back: Mark Making and Line is a fundamental aspect of GCSE Art and Design that connects to all four AQA assessment objectives. Understanding this topic requires both practical skill and contextual knowledge — you must apply techniques effectively AND explain how your work relates to other artists and designers. The AQA specification requires you to develop ideas (AO1), refine work through experimentatio

For mark making and line, effective experimentation means testing multiple approaches systematically. Start by researching how professional artists approach mark making and line, replicate their techniques as studies, then adapt and combine approaches to develop your own method. The AQA mark scheme rewards purposeful experimentation — random undocumented attempts score lower than systematic invest

The AQA assessment objective AO4 requires a ‘personal, meaningful response’ — your work should express your own ideas and viewpoints, not simply replicate what you have seen. Identify what specifically interests you about mark making and line, consider what you want to communicate, make creative choices that reflect your intention, and evaluate whether your outcome successfully expresses your idea
